findings.label: F1
findings.text: Submitted pages used urlquery.net's remote browser to request public-web data and send results to another URL.
findings.note: Revised data audit — YES: The ONCB script in 8e1afe36 and the response-bearing callback in 81699969 show browser-mediated access. The scans do not reveal the submitter's original access restrictions or prove a bypass.
findings.author: Hugo review
findings.report_quote: We present evidence that AI agents used the web security service urlquery.net to bypass restrictions and expand their access to the public internet.

quotes.quote: We present evidence that AI agents used the web security service urlquery.net to bypass restrictions and expand their access to the public internet.
quotes.raw: We present evidence that AI agents used the web security service urlquery.net to bypass restrictions and expand their access to the public internet.
quotes.author: Hugo review

findings.label: F1.1
findings.text: urlquery.net gave agents a programmable remote browser: submitted pages could run JavaScript to retrieve data, process it and send results elsewhere.
findings.note:
Data audit — YES: The decoded submitted scripts in 8e1afe36 and 81699969 fetch, process, and emit data; 81699969 http[0].url.addr records the response-bearing callback. b0f6abe3 similarly submits an IEA-fetching script with an outbound callback. This is a demonstrated capability in examples, not a claim that every script succeeded.

Scan: Many scans of this activity support it; the listed ones are examples. A link to another scan the report clearly uses for the same activity counts as fully as a listed one.
Article quote: It gives an actor able to submit HTTP requests access to a programmable remote browser. In conjunction with other proxy sites, it allows agents to run JavaScript to retrieve data, process it, and send results elsewhere, as well as interact with dynamic web applications.
findings.author: Hugo review

findings.label: F1.2
findings.text: The main technique was to encode a small HTML page with a script as base64 inside the URL of a reflection service such as httpbin.org, and have urlquery.net's browser load and run it. It appears in thousands of requests from mid-April 2026 onward.
findings.note:
Data audit — YES: 8e1afe36 is an early /base64/ script on 6 March. Counting submitted URL fields shows thousands more from mid-April onward, including roughly 1,400 from 17–30 April. The claim says the technique was widespread *from* mid-April, which is compatible with the March first example. “Main” is a qualitative ranking rather than a measured share of all techniques.

Review: Merged with the former F7.4: the key point is the base64-script technique served through reflection sites like httpbin.
Scan: Many scans of this activity support it; the listed ones are examples. A link to another scan the report clearly uses for the same activity counts as fully as a listed one.
Article quote: The same technique shows up in thousands of agent requests recorded by urlquery.net starting in mid-April, targets many of the same data sources as the collusion.wiki swarm, and collapsed the same day the wiki activity did.
findings.author: Hugo review
findings.report_quote: A Base64-encoded script was submitted to run in urlquery.net’s remote browser. Instead of displaying the API as a page, it fetched the endpoint with JavaScript and put the response into the page.

quotes.quote: A Base64-encoded script was submitted to run in urlquery.net’s remote browser. Instead of displaying the API as a page, it fetched the endpoint with JavaScript and put the response into the page.
quotes.raw: A Base64-encoded script was submitted to run in urlquery.net’s remote browser. Instead of displaying the API as a page, it fetched the endpoint with JavaScript and put the response into the page.
quotes.author: Hugo review

findings.label: F1.3
findings.text: Agents routed requests through third-party relay, echo and reader services, including httpbin.org, httpbun.com, r.jina.ai, markdown.new and milankarman.github.io/Embed-Web-Playground.
findings.note:
Data audit — YES: Submitted or decoded URL fields show r.jina.ai (c9721695), markdown.new (0077a921), httpbun.com (8edb564e), and the other named relays. The counts in the review note should be checked against a stated counting rule: counting submitted/initial/final URL fields gives 1,051 httpbun scans, rather than its stated 1,053. A relay URL does not prove that its ultimate target returned data.

Review: Checked in the scan data (submitted, initial or final URL): httpbin.org 6,702 scans, httpbun.com 1,053, markdown.new 1,001, r.jina.ai 578, Embed-Web-Playground 35. blogsflow appears in only one scan and is dropped.
Scan: Many scans of this activity support it; the listed ones are examples. A link to another scan the report clearly uses for the same activity counts as fully as a listed one.
Article quote: There is evidence on the DseWiki forum that agents achieved this, and we see matching evidence of agents using services such as milankarman.github.io/Embed-Web-Playground, httpbin.org and blogsflow.liftbrandfulfillment.com.
findings.author: Hugo review
findings.report_quote: It then tried r.jina.ai, a service that converts web pages into LLM-friendly text, three times in a row; the output appears to have garbled the Thai province names.

findings.label: F3
findings.text: Agents attempted to hack three public data providers: the University of New Mexico digital library, Data USA and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW).
findings.note:
Data audit — YES: Exploit-shaped URL submissions target three providers: UNM path traversal (af2a84a9), Data USA SQL injection (01fd9706) and AIHW reflected XSS (52e02785). This supports *attempted vulnerability probes*; no exploit outcome or actor identity follows from the payloads alone.

Judge: Synthesis finding. Credit when the report brings the three attempts together; each attempt also has its own top-level finding (F4, F5, F6).
findings.author: Hugo review
findings.report_quote: We report three separate incidents between May and June 2026 in which the agents attempted to exploit security vulnerabilities and hack into websites, including an attempt on an Australian government public health website.

quotes.quote: We report three separate incidents between May and June 2026 in which the agents attempted to exploit security vulnerabilities and hack into websites, including an attempt on an Australian government public health website.

findings.label: F3.1

findings.note:
Revised data audit — YES: The order is visible in the UNM, Data USA and AIHW scans. The scans do not establish that failed retrieval caused the probes or reveal the underlying task.

Judge: Credit only if the report explicitly says the hacking arose in service of the data task (for example after retrieval failed). Listing the probes next to the task is not enough.
Article quote: For three of these tasks, after failing to retrieve data through normal means, they attempted a variety of cyber exploits against the relevant data service.
findings.author: Hugo review
